newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish government wins budget, loses partner.
newsitem.headline: Danish government wins budget, loses partner.

text.p: Denmark's minority government won a two-month battle to get its 1997 finance bill through parliament on Thursday night but on Friday lost a coalition partner alarmed by the far left's role in the budget fight.
Announcing their departure "as soon as is convenient" on Friday, the Centre Democrats said that their five members of parliament would continue to vote with the government.
Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen said that he would reshuffle the rump coalition of his Social Democrats and the smaller Radical Liberals in January.

He will need to replace Trade Minister Mimi Jakobsen and health minister Yvonne Herloev Andersen. Centre Democrat leader Jakobsen said her party could not live with an alliance with two far left parties, which ensured the budget's passage.

"I must characterise the outlook for 1997 as one in which the government must work with shifting majorities and in an increasing number of cases be dependent on the Socialist People's Party and the Unity List," she said in a statement.
Parliament approved the finance bill by 129 votes to seven on Thursday as a result of government deals with the two leftist parties who hold the balance of power in the 179-seat house.
The anti-establishment Unity List abstained after having earlier considered voting against the budget.

The Socialist People's Party (SPP), which has voted against every budget since 1982, backed the 1997 proposal in exchange for government pledges to fund adult education, job retraining, social, environmental and cultural projects and improved workplace conditions.

The opposition Conservatives and Liberals, unable to secure a majority vote against the ruling coalition, joined the left in voting for the budget but remain committed to toppling the government at the first opportunity.

A recent poll of decision-makers at the country's biggest institutional investors showed more than 40 percent convinced that the coalition, commanding 76 seats with the Centre Democrats' continued support, to the right-wing opposition's combined 83, would fall within a year.
An opinion poll in the tabloid daily BT on Friday showed the Social Democrats winning 50 seats if an election were held now, compared to their present 62.
Former foreign minister Uffe Ellemann-Jensen's Liberal were seen as increasing their 42 seats to 51, becoming the largest single party in parliament.

The government, despite public misgivings from the Centre Democrats, began wooing the left after budget talks with the Conservatives collapsed on November 1 over government plans to balance the budget through higher taxes.
It plans to finance its pledges to the SPP and turn the previously forecast 3.5 billion crown ($973.8 million) public sector budget deficit into surplus largely by one-off measures.

One is the liquidation of a state insurance fund against marine war damages estimated to contain some 3.5 billion crowns. Other funding is to come from the sale of state property holdings and the transfer of money from a workers' holiday fund.
Unlike some European neighbours Denmark has no need of an austerity drive to meet entrance criteria for Economic and Monetary Union as it already qualifies.
But Danes voted against joining EMU in a 1993 referendum and a fresh plebiscite -- for which the government says it has no plans -- would be required for Danish membership.
